question: What was the federal funds target range after each FOMC meeting in 2025, and at which meetings did the Committee change it?
answer:
Taking "each FOMC meeting in 2025" to mean the eight scheduled meetings in the collection (Jan 28-29, Mar 18-19, May 6-7, Jun 17-18, Jul 29-30, Sep 16-17, Oct 28-29, Dec 9-10), the Committee held the federal funds target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent for the first five meetings and then cut it by 25 basis points at each of the last three, ending the year at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. The three meetings that changed the range were September 16-17, October 28-29, and December 9-10, 2025, each a 1/4 percentage point cut.

| Meeting (2025) | Target range after meeting | Change? |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 28-29 (statement Jan 29) | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | No — held [D16] |
| Mar 18-19 (statement Mar 19) | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | No — held [D23] |
| May 6-7 (statement May 7) | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | No — held [D17] |
| Jun 17-18 (statement Jun 18) | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | No — held [D18] |
| Jul 29-30 (statement Jul 30) | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | No — held [D19] |
| Sep 16-17 (statement Sep 17) | 4 to 4-1/4 percent | Yes — cut 1/4 pp (25 bps) [D20] |
| Oct 28-29 (statement Oct 29) | 3-3/4 to 4 percent | Yes — cut 1/4 pp (25 bps) [D21] |
| Dec 9-10 (statement Dec 10) | 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent | Yes — cut 1/4 pp (25 bps) [D22] |

Supporting detail:
- The first five meetings (January through July) each "maintain[ed] the target range for the federal funds rate at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent," so no change occurred at any of them [D16][D23][D17][D18][D19].
- At the September 16-17 meeting, the Committee "decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 4 to 4-1/4 percent," citing a shift in the balance of risks with downside risks to employment having risen [D20].
- At the October 28-29 meeting, it again "lower[ed] the target range ... by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent" [D21].
- At the December 9-10 meeting, it "lower[ed] the target range ... by 1/4 percentage point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent" [D22].

Notes on voting (not rate changes, but relevant context): at the March meeting, Christopher J. Waller voted against the action over the pace of securities-holdings reduction, not the rate [D23]; at the July meeting, Michelle W. Bowman and Christopher J. Waller dissented, preferring a 1/4 pp cut [D19]; at the September, October, and December meetings, Stephen I. Miran dissented preferring a 1/2 pp cut, and at the latter two, Jeffrey R. Schmid (and at December, Austan D. Goolsbee) dissented preferring no change [D20][D21][D22].

The evidence covers all eight meetings in the collection; no 2025 meeting is missing.

question: Who dissented at each FOMC meeting in 2025, and what did each dissenter prefer?
answer:
Taking "each FOMC meeting in 2025" to mean all eight scheduled 2025 meetings (January 28–29, March 18–19, May 6–7, June 17–18, July 29–30, September 16–17, October 28–29, and December 9–10): five meetings had dissents and three were unanimous. The dissenters and what they preferred, in time order, are:

| Meeting (2025) | Action | Dissenter(s) | What the dissenter(s) preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 28–29 | Hold at 4¼–4½% | None — unanimous (12 for) | — [D40][D18] |
| Mar 18–19 | Hold at 4¼–4½%; slowed balance-sheet runoff | Christopher J. Waller (Board Governor) | No change to the federal funds target range, but to continue the current pace of securities-holdings decline (i.e., opposed slowing the runoff) [D41][D20] |
| May 6–7 | Hold at 4¼–4½% | None — unanimous (12 for; Neel Kashkari as alternate) | — [D42][D24] |
| Jun 17–18 | Hold at 4¼–4½% | None — unanimous (12 for) | — [D43][D27] |
| Jul 29–30 | Hold at 4¼–4½% | Michelle W. Bowman (Board Governor) and Christopher J. Waller (Board Governor) | Both preferred to lower the target range by ¼ percentage point at this meeting (Adriana D. Kugler was absent and not voting) [D44][D30] |
| Sep 16–17 | Cut ¼ point to 4–4¼% | Stephen I. Miran (Board Governor) | Preferred to lower the target range by ½ percentage point at this meeting [D45][D31] |
| Oct 28–29 | Cut ¼ point to 3¾–4% | Stephen I. Miran (Board Governor) and Jeffrey R. Schmid (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis) | Miran preferred a ½-point cut; Schmid preferred no change to the target range [D46][D35] |
| Dec 9–10 | Cut ¼ point to 3½–3¾% | Stephen I. Miran (Board Governor); Austan D. Goolsbee (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago) and Jeffrey R. Schmid (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis) | Miran preferred a ½-point cut; Goolsbee and Schmid preferred no change to the target range [D47][D39]

Supporting detail:
- The three unanimous meetings (January, May, June) are confirmed by the minutes' "Voting against this action: None" and by the statements listing all twelve voting members in favor [D40][D18][D42][D24][D43][D27].
- The March dissent was the only one tied to the balance-sheet decision rather than the rate: the minutes note Waller's view was based on reserve balances being over $3 trillion and no evidence the banking system was near an ample level of reserves [D20].
- The July minutes add that Governor Bowman's preference for a 25-basis-point cut to 4–4¼% reflected inflation moving closer to the 2% objective (excluding temporary tariff effects), a labor market near full employment but with less dynamism, and slowing growth [D30].
- The October minutes note that one of the two dissenters also preferred an immediate end to balance-sheet runoff, though the statement does not specify which [D35].

Note on titles: the FOMC statements name dissenters without titles; the titles above (Board Governor vs. Federal Reserve Bank President) are taken from the minutes' attendance lists and standard FOMC roles. All eight meetings' statements and minutes were covered, so no 2025 meeting is left unaddressed.

Of the 8 FOMC meetings in 2025, five had dissents (March, July, September, October, December) and three were unanimous (January, May, June). Details meeting by meeting:

1) January 28-29, 2025 (hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%): No dissents — all 12 voting members voted for the action; the minutes state "Voting against this action: None" [D40][D18].

2) March 18-19, 2025 (hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; slowed balance-sheet runoff): One dissent — Christopher J. Waller, Board Governor, voted against. He preferred no change to the federal funds target range but preferred to continue the current pace of securities-holdings decline (i.e., he opposed slowing the runoff) [D41][D20].

3) May 6-7, 2025 (hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%): No dissents — all 12 voted for the action (Neel Kashkari voted as an alternate member) [D42][D24].

4) June 17-18, 2025 (hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%): No dissents — all 12 voted for the action; minutes state "Voting against this action: None" [D43][D27].

5) July 29-30, 2025 (hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%): Two dissents — Michelle W. Bowman (Board Governor) and Christopher J. Waller (Board Governor), who preferred to lower the target range by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting. Adriana D. Kugler was absent and not voting [D44][D30].

6) September 16-17, 2025 (cut 1/4 point to 4 to 4-1/4%): One dissent — Stephen I. Miran, Board Governor, who preferred to lower the target range by 1/2 percentage point at this meeting [D45][D31].

7) October 28-29, 2025 (cut 1/4 point to 3-3/4 to 4%): Two dissents — Stephen I. Miran (Board Governor), who preferred a 1/2 percentage point cut, and Jeffrey R. Schmid (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis), who preferred no change to the target range [D46][D35].

8) December 9-10, 2025 (cut 1/4 point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%): Three dissents — Stephen I. Miran (Board Governor), who preferred a 1/2 percentage point cut; and Austan D. Goolsbee (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago) and Jeffrey R. Schmid (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis), who preferred no change to the target range [D47][D39].

Note on titles: the statements name dissenters without titles; titles are from the minutes' attendance lists and standard FOMC roles (Bowman, Waller, Miran = Board Governors; Schmid = Minneapolis Fed President; Goolsbee = Chicago Fed President).

question: How did the Beige Book's overall assessment of economic activity change across the eight editions of 2024?
answer:
Taking the question to mean the National Summary's "Overall Economic Activity" subsection of each of the eight 2024 Beige Book editions, the overall assessment traced a clear arc: a flat, holiday-lifted start; a gradual build to a mid-year peak of expansion; a sharp summer-to-early-fall slowdown; and a modest year-end rebound.

| Edition (date) | Overall assessment of activity | Key tone / notable shifts |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 17, 2024 | A majority of Districts reported "little or no change"; three at modest growth, one at a moderate decline [D29] | Holiday consumer spending met/exceeded expectations; manufacturing fell in nearly all Districts; optimism from the prospect of falling rates; uncertainty from the office market, weakening demand, and the 2024 political cycle [D29] |
| Mar 6, 2024 | Activity "increased slightly, on balance" (8 Districts slight-to-modest growth, 3 no change, 1 slight softening) [D30] | Consumer spending inched down with heightened price sensitivity and trade-down behavior; Red Sea/Panama Canal shipping disruptions; a pickup in residential real estate [D30] |
| Apr 17, 2024 | Activity "expanded slightly, on balance" (10 of 12 Districts slight/modest growth, up from 8) [D7] | Consumer spending barely increased and was mixed, with continued weakness in discretionary spending; manufacturing declined slightly [D7] |
| May 29, 2024 | Activity "continued to expand" (most Districts slight/modest growth, 2 no change) — the year's peak [D31] | Outlook "grew somewhat more pessimistic amid reports of rising uncertainty and greater downside risks" [D31] |
| Jul 17, 2024 | Activity maintained "a slight to modest pace of growth in a majority of Districts," but flat/declining Districts rose to five (three more than the prior period) [D32] | Expectations for slower growth over six months due to election, domestic policy, geopolitical conflict, and inflation uncertainty [D32] |
| Sep 4, 2024 | The turning point: only three Districts grew slightly, while flat/declining Districts jumped from five to nine [D33] | Consumer spending "ticked down in most Districts"; manufacturing declined in most Districts; layoffs remained rare [D33] |
| Oct 23, 2024 | Activity "little changed in nearly all Districts" (only two at modest growth) [D25] | The short-lived dockworkers strike caused only minor disruptions; Hurricane damage hit the Southeast; contacts were "somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook" [D25] |
| Dec 4, 2024 | Activity "rose slightly in most Districts" (three at modest/moderate growth offsetting two flat/declining) [D27] | Expectations for growth rose moderately; contacts optimistic that demand would rise; consumer spending stable but price sensitivity kept rising [D27] |

**How the assessment evolved.** The year opened flat (January), improved to slight expansion (March–April), reached its peak of broad expansion in May, then decelerated over the summer and into early fall, with the September edition marking the clearest turning point as a majority of Districts reported flat or declining activity. The October edition showed stabilization ("little changed"), and the December edition recorded a modest rebound with slightly higher growth expectations.

**Consistent themes across the year.** (1) Consumer price sensitivity and trade-down behavior, first flagged in March and persisting through December [D30][D27]; (2) a cooling labor market with easing tightness, lower turnover, and slowing wage growth (wages "modest to moderate" early, "modest" by fall) [D29][D33][D27]; (3) manufacturing weakness/declines [D29][D33]; (4) high interest rates constraining auto and housing [D29][D33]; and (5) office/commercial real estate weakness contrasted with strong data-center demand [D30][D25].

**Tariffs.** Tariffs were essentially absent from the "Overall Economic Activity" subsections for most of 2024. They first appear in the December edition's Prices subsection, where businesses "indicated tariffs pose a significant upside risk to inflation," and in the Philadelphia District note on inflation expectations edging higher "over concerns about potential tariffs" [D28].

The main turning points were the May→July→September deceleration (expansion giving way to a majority of flat/declining Districts) and the October→December stabilization and modest rebound.

data.answer:
Across the eight 2024 Beige Book editions, the National Summary's "Overall Economic Activity" subsection traced a clear arc from a flat, holiday-lifted start to a mid-year peak of expansion, a sharp summer/early-fall slowdown, and a modest year-end rebound. January 17: a majority of Districts reported "little or no change," with three at modest growth and one at a moderate decline; holiday consumer spending was a bright spot, manufacturing fell nearly everywhere, and optimism centered on the prospect of falling interest rates, while the office market, weakening demand, and the 2024 political cycle were cited as uncertainty sources [D29]. March 6: activity "increased slightly, on balance" (8 Districts slight-to-modest growth, 3 no change, 1 slight softening); consumer spending inched down with heightened price sensitivity and trade-down behavior; Red Sea/Panama Canal shipping disruptions and a pickup in residential real estate were noted [D30]. April 17: activity "expanded slightly" (10 of 12 Districts slight/modest growth, up from 8); consumer spending barely increased and was mixed, with continued weakness in discretionary spending [D7]. May 29: activity "continued to expand" (most Districts slight/modest growth, 2 no change) — the peak of the year — but the outlook "grew somewhat more pessimistic amid reports of rising uncertainty and greater downside risks" [D31]. July 17: activity maintained "a slight to modest pace of growth in a majority of Districts," but flat/declining Districts rose to five (three more than prior period); expectations pointed to slower growth over six months due to election, policy, geopolitical, and inflation uncertainty [D32]. September 4: the clear turning point — only three Districts grew slightly while flat/declining Districts jumped from five to nine; consumer spending "ticked down in most Districts" and manufacturing declined in most Districts, though layoffs remained rare [D33]. October 23: activity "little changed in nearly all Districts" (only two at modest growth); the short-lived dockworkers strike caused only minor disruptions and Hurricane damage hit the Southeast, but contacts were "somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook" [D25]. December 4: activity "rose slightly in most Districts" (three at modest/moderate growth offsetting two flat/declining), with expectations for growth rising moderately and contacts optimistic that demand would rise; consumer spending was stable but price sensitivity kept rising [D27].

Consistent themes all year: (1) consumer price sensitivity and trade-down behavior, first flagged in March and persisting through December; (2) a cooling labor market with easing tightness, lower turnover, and slowing wage growth (wages "modest to moderate" early, "modest" by fall); (3) manufacturing weakness/declines; (4) high interest rates constraining auto and housing; (5) the office/commercial real estate weakness contrasted with strong data-center demand. Tariffs were essentially absent from the "Overall Economic Activity" subsections for most of the year; they first appear in the December edition's Prices subsection, where businesses "indicated tariffs pose a significant upside risk to inflation" [D28], and in the Philadelphia District note on higher inflation expectations "over concerns about potential tariffs" [D28]. The main turning points were the May→July→September deceleration (expansion giving way to a majority of flat/declining Districts) and the October→December stabilization/rebound.

question: How did the Financial Stability Reports from May 2023 to May 2026 characterize asset valuations?
answer:
Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) from May 2023 through May 2026, the Committee’s characterization of asset valuations escalated from "moderate" to "elevated," with a temporary softening to "notable" in April 2025 before returning to "elevated." Throughout this period, equities and residential real estate remained at or near historical highs relative to fundamentals, while commercial real estate (CRE) was the persistent weak spot, showing signs of stabilization only from April 2025 onward.

### Evolution of Overall Characterizations

The section headings and opening summaries of each FSR track the Committee’s shifting assessment of valuation pressures:

| Report Date | Overall Characterization | Key Context |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **May 2023** | "Asset valuation pressures remained moderate despite notable fluctuations in financial markets" [D3][D22] | Pressures were elevated in property markets but moderate overall, despite March 2023 bank failures [D3]. |
| **October 2023** | "Asset valuation pressures rose to a notable level" [D5][D25] | Equity valuations increased from an already high level; property prices remained elevated relative to fundamentals [D5]. |
| **April 2024** | "Asset valuations increased to elevated levels relative to fundamentals" [D8][D28] | Equity valuations increased further; corporate bond valuations appeared stretched [D8]. |
| **November 2024** | "Asset valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals" [D12][D31] | Valuations continued to rise in equities; corporate debt remained stretched [D12]. |
| **April 2025** | "Asset valuations were notable despite price declines in some markets in early April" [D14][D34] | U.S. trade-policy announcements sparked declines, but prices remained high relative to fundamentals [D34]. |
| **November 2025** | "Asset valuations were elevated, with some markets setting new highs after recovering from April’s declines" [D17][D37] | Price declines largely reversed; volatility receded [D17]. |
| **May 2026** | "Asset valuations remained elevated, although risk premiums increased in several markets amid periods of higher volatility" [D40] | Valuations stayed at the high end of their ranges; Treasury term premiums increased [D40]. |

### Asset Class Specifics

The reports consistently highlighted four main asset classes: equities, corporate credit, residential real estate, and commercial real estate (CRE), with farmland and Treasury securities also discussed.

**Equities**
*   **May 2023:** Forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio was "notably above its historical average" [D24].
*   **October 2023:** Forward P/E rose to a level "further above its historical median"; equity premium was "well below historical norms" [D25][D27].
*   **April 2024:** Forward P/E sat in the "upper end of its historical distribution since 1989"; equity premium was "well below its historical median" [D30].
*   **November 2024:** Forward P/E "continued to climb" from the upper end of its range; equity premium remained "well below its historical median" [D33].
*   **April 2025:** Despite a >6% price decline through April 11, equity prices "remained high relative to forecasted earnings"; forward P/E was "well above its historical median" [D34][D36].
*   **November 2025:** Forward P/E "remained well above its historical median"; equity premium "remained well below its historical median" [D39].
*   **May 2026:** Forward P/E "remained well above its historical median" (in the upper range of its historical distribution); equity premium "moved up a touch from an overall low level" [D42][D44].

**Corporate Credit**
*   **May 2023:** Spreads were "near their historical averages" [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads were "somewhat below their historical averages" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations "appeared stretched"; spreads fell to levels in the "lower range of their historical distributions" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Corporate debt markets "remained stretched" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads "widened significantly but have stayed at or below their historical medians" [D34].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads "stayed well below their historical medians" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Spreads "continued to be low by historical standards" [D40].

**Residential Real Estate**
*   **May 2023:** Valuations "remained near all-time highs" [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Prices relative to rents "remained near all-time highs" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations "remained near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Valuations "remained near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals "continued to be well above their historical averages" [D14][D34].
*   **November 2025:** Prices "continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals but at a lower rate" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Prices "remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals"; price-to-rent ratio was "in the upper ranges of its historical distribution" [D40][D44].

**Commercial Real Estate (CRE)**
*   **May 2023:** Valuations "remained near historical highs" despite widespread price declines; fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Fundamentals in office properties were "especially weak" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Market conditions "continued to deteriorate, especially for the office sector" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Conditions "continued to deteriorate, especially for the office and multifamily sectors" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Markets showed "some signs of stabilizing prices and fundamentals" [D34].
*   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed "continued signs of stabilizing" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Markets showed "continued signs of stabilizing," though vulnerabilities due to upcoming refinancing needs remained [D40][D44].

### Key Drivers and Risks

The primary drivers and risks cited in the reports shifted over time:
*   **2023:** The March 2023 bank failures (SVB, Signature) caused notable strains in short-term Treasury market liquidity and heightened uncertainty [D3][D22].
*   **2023–2024:** Low Treasury market liquidity was repeatedly cited as a factor that could "amplify the impact of shocks on asset valuations" [D8][D12].
*   **August 2024:** The unwind of the yen-carry trade contributed to a temporary spike in market volatility [D12][D31].
*   **April 2025:** U.S. trade-policy announcements triggered a broad sell-off, with equity prices falling >6% and option-implied volatility reaching levels not seen since March 2020 [D34][D36].
*   **2025–2026:** CRE refinancing risk remained a persistent vulnerability [D17][D40]. By May 2026, rising Treasury term premiums amid volatility, partly due to geopolitical tensions, were noted [D40][D44].

Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (May 2023 → May 2026), the Asset Valuations section shows a clear escalation from "moderate" to "elevated" that has persisted, with a temporary softening in April 2025. The section heading/characterization evolved as follows: May 2023 "Asset valuation pressures remained moderate despite notable fluctuations in financial markets" [D3]; October 2023 "Asset valuation pressures rose to a notable level" [D5]; April 2024 "Asset valuations increased to elevated levels relative to fundamentals" [D8]; November 2024 "Asset valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals" [D12]; April 2025 "Asset valuations were notable despite price declines in some markets in early April" [D14]; November 2025 "Asset valuations were elevated, with some markets setting new highs after recovering from April's declines" [D17]; May 2026 "Asset valuations remained elevated, although risk premiums increased in several markets amid periods of higher volatility" [D40].

The four asset classes consistently highlighted were equities, corporate credit (bonds/loans), residential real estate, and commercial real estate (CRE), with Treasury securities and farmland also discussed. Equities: forward P/E rose from "notably above its historical average" (May 2023) to the "upper end of its historical distribution" (April 2024) and stayed there through May 2026, while the equity premium stayed "well below its historical median" throughout. Corporate credit: spreads moved from "near historical averages" (May 2023) to "stretched"/"low by historical standards" (April 2024 onward). Residential real estate: valuations "near all-time highs" (May 2023) to "near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s" (April/Nov 2024) to "well above their historical relationship with fundamentals" (2025-2026). CRE: the persistent weak spot, with deteriorating conditions (especially office) in 2023-2024, then "signs of stabilizing" from April 2025 onward, though refinancing/distressed-sale risk remained.

Key drivers/risks shifted over time: early 2023 was dominated by the SVB/Signature/First Republic bank failures and the resulting March 2023 liquidity strains in short-term Treasuries [D22]; 2023-2024 emphasized low Treasury market liquidity amplifying shocks and, by November 2024, the yen-carry trade unwind that spiked August 2024 volatility [D12]; April 2025 was driven by U.S. trade-policy announcements causing a broad sell-off (equities fell >6% through April 11, volatility hit levels not seen since March 2020) [D34][D36]; and 2025-2026 emphasized CRE refinancing risk and, by May 2026, rising Treasury term premiums amid volatility partly from geopolitical tensions [D40][D44].

Across the seven Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) from May 2023 through May 2026, the Committee’s characterization of asset valuations escalated from "moderate" to "elevated," with a temporary softening to "notable" in April 2025 before returning to "elevated." Throughout this period, equities and residential real estate remained at or near historical highs relative to fundamentals, while commercial real estate (CRE) was the persistent weak spot, showing signs of stabilization only from April 2025 onward.

### Evolution of Overall Characterizations

The section headings and opening summaries of each FSR track the Committee’s shifting assessment of valuation pressures:

| Report Date | Overall Characterization | Key Context |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **May 2023** | "Asset valuation pressures remained moderate despite notable fluctuations in financial markets" [D3][D22] | Pressures were elevated in property markets but moderate overall, despite March 2023 bank failures [D3]. |
| **October 2023** | "Asset valuation pressures rose to a notable level" [D5][D25] | Equity valuations increased from an already high level; property prices remained elevated relative to fundamentals [D5]. |
| **April 2024** | "Asset valuations increased to elevated levels relative to fundamentals" [D8][D28] | Equity valuations increased further; corporate bond valuations appeared stretched [D8]. |
| **November 2024** | "Asset valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals" [D12][D31] | Valuations continued to rise in equities; corporate debt remained stretched [D12]. |
| **April 2025** | "Asset valuations were notable despite price declines in some markets in early April" [D14][D34] | U.S. trade-policy announcements sparked declines, but prices remained high relative to fundamentals [D34]. |
| **November 2025** | "Asset valuations were elevated, with some markets setting new highs after recovering from April’s declines" [D17][D37] | Price declines largely reversed; volatility receded [D17]. |
| **May 2026** | "Asset valuations remained elevated, although risk premiums increased in several markets amid periods of higher volatility" [D40] | Valuations stayed at the high end of their ranges; Treasury term premiums increased [D40]. |

### Asset Class Specifics

The reports consistently highlighted four main asset classes: equities, corporate credit, residential real estate, and commercial real estate (CRE), with farmland and Treasury securities also discussed.

**Equities**
*   **May 2023:** Forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio was "notably above its historical average" [D24].
*   **October 2023:** Forward P/E rose to a level "further above its historical median"; equity premium was "well below historical norms" [D25][D27].
*   **April 2024:** Forward P/E sat in the "upper end of its historical distribution since 1989"; equity premium was "well below its historical median" [D30].
*   **November 2024:** Forward P/E "continued to climb" from the upper end of its range; equity premium remained "well below its historical median" [D33].
*   **April 2025:** Despite a >6% price decline through April 11, equity prices "remained high relative to forecasted earnings"; forward P/E was "well above its historical median" [D34][D36].
*   **November 2025:** Forward P/E "remained well above its historical median"; equity premium "remained well below its historical median" [D39].
*   **May 2026:** Forward P/E "remained well above its historical median" (in the upper range of its historical distribution); equity premium "moved up a touch from an overall low level" [D42][D44].

**Corporate Credit**
*   **May 2023:** Spreads were "near their historical averages" [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads were "somewhat below their historical averages" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations "appeared stretched"; spreads fell to levels in the "lower range of their historical distributions" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Corporate debt markets "remained stretched" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads "widened significantly but have stayed at or below their historical medians" [D34].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads "stayed well below their historical medians" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Spreads "continued to be low by historical standards" [D40].

**Residential Real Estate**
*   **May 2023:** Valuations "remained near all-time highs" [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Prices relative to rents "remained near all-time highs" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Valuations "remained near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Valuations "remained near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals "continued to be well above their historical averages" [D14][D34].
*   **November 2025:** Prices "continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals but at a lower rate" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Prices "remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals"; price-to-rent ratio was "in the upper ranges of its historical distribution" [D40][D44].

**Commercial Real Estate (CRE)**
*   **May 2023:** Valuations "remained near historical highs" despite widespread price declines; fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D3].
*   **October 2023:** Fundamentals in office properties were "especially weak" [D5].
*   **April 2024:** Market conditions "continued to deteriorate, especially for the office sector" [D8].
*   **November 2024:** Conditions "continued to deteriorate, especially for the office and multifamily sectors" [D12].
*   **April 2025:** Markets showed "some signs of stabilizing prices and fundamentals" [D34].
*   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed "continued signs of stabilizing" [D17].
*   **May 2026:** Markets showed "continued signs of stabilizing," though vulnerabilities due to upcoming refinancing needs remained [D40][D44].

### Key Drivers and Risks

The primary drivers and risks cited in the reports shifted over time:
*   **2023:** The March 2023 bank failures (SVB, Signature) caused notable strains in short-term Treasury market liquidity and heightened uncertainty [D3][D22].
*   **2023–2024:** Low Treasury market liquidity was repeatedly cited as a factor that could "amplify the impact of shocks on asset valuations" [D8][D12].
*   **August 2024:** The unwind of the yen-carry trade contributed to a temporary spike in market volatility [D12][D31].
*   **April 2025:** U.S. trade-policy announcements triggered a broad sell-off, with equity prices falling >6% and option-implied volatility reaching levels not seen since March 2020 [D34][D36].
*   **2025–2026:** CRE refinancing risk remained a persistent vulnerability [D17][D40]. By May 2026, rising Treasury term premiums amid volatility, partly due to geopolitical tensions, were noted [D40][D44].

question: How did FOMC participants' median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate change across the Summaries of Economic Projections from March 2025 to September 2026?
answer:
The FOMC's median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate declined by 0.2 percentage points over the period, moving from 4.3% in the March 19, 2025 Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) to 4.1% in the September 16, 2026 SEP [D1]. The path was not monotonic: it first rose to a peak of 4.5% in June 2025, then eased and held steady before falling in the second half of 2026 [D1].

| SEP release date | Median 2026 unemployment rate | Change vs. prior SEP |
|---|---|---|
| March 19, 2025 | 4.3% | — |
| June 18, 2025 | 4.5% | +0.2 pp |
| September 17, 2025 | 4.4% | −0.1 pp |
| December 10, 2025 | 4.4% | unchanged |
| March 18, 2026 | 4.4% | unchanged |
| June 17, 2026 | 4.3% | −0.1 pp |
| September 16, 2026 | 4.1% | −0.2 pp |

Source: median (50th percentile) "Unemployment rate" row for the 2026 horizon in Table 1 of each SEP [D1].

Step-by-step:
- March 19, 2025: 4.3% [D1]
- June 18, 2025: 4.5%, up 0.2 pp — the high point of the period [D1]
- September 17, 2025: 4.4%, down 0.1 pp [D1]
- December 10, 2025: 4.4%, unchanged [D1]
- March 18, 2026: 4.4%, unchanged (second consecutive hold) [D1]
- June 17, 2026: 4.3%, down 0.1 pp [D1]
- September 16, 2026: 4.1%, down 0.2 pp [D1]

Net change from March 2025 to September 2026 was a decline of 0.2 pp (4.3% → 4.1%), with the trajectory peaking at 4.5% in June 2025 [D1].

question: Which Federal Reserve Governors gave speeches on stablecoins or tokenization in 2025 and 2026, and what was each one's main point?
answer:
Based on the evidence provided, two Federal Reserve Governors gave speeches addressing stablecoins or tokenization in 2025 and 2026: Governor Lisa D. Cook and Governor Christopher J. Waller.

**Governor Lisa D. Cook**
*   **Speech:** "An Assessment of the Economy and Financial Stability"
*   **Venue:** Seventh Conference on Law and Macroeconomics, University of Michigan Law School, Ann Arbor, Michigan [D1].
*   **Main Point:** Governor Cook emphasized that while stablecoins currently have a relatively small footprint in the U.S. (approximately $170 billion in assets under management) and are primarily used for digital asset investments rather than real economic transactions, they pose significant financial stability risks [D1]. Her main argument focused on the structural vulnerability of stablecoins to "runs" due to their peg to reference assets, noting that a run on a large stablecoin could disrupt funding markets like commercial paper or certificates of deposit if the backing assets are liquidated [D2]. She also highlighted the lack of a comprehensive federal regulatory framework for stablecoins and the risks associated with their use in intermediation chains, such as serving as loan collateral [D2].

**Governor Christopher J. Waller**
*   **Speech:** "Reflections on a Maturing Stablecoin Market"
*   **Venue:** A Very Stable Conference, San Francisco, California [D4].
*   **Main Point:** Governor Waller argued that for stablecoins to reach their full potential in improving retail and cross-border payments, they must demonstrate both a clear use case and a clear commercial case [D4]. He distinguished between the two, noting that a use case is necessary to attract consumers and businesses, while a viable business model is essential for issuers to continue operating [D4]. His speech focused on examining the challenges and roadblocks that could impede stablecoins from achieving scale as the market matures [D4].

*Note: The evidence provided does not contain specific dates for these speeches, only the venues and titles. Additionally, the evidence does not cover any other Federal Reserve Governors who may have spoken on these topics during the 2025–2026 period.*

question: How did the Monetary Policy Reports from February 2025 to July 2026 describe the role of tariffs in inflation?
answer:
Taking "Monetary Policy Reports from February 2025 to July 2026" to mean the three MPRs available in that window—February 7, 2025; June 20, 2025; and July 10, 2026—the reports show a clear evolution: from no explicit tariff-inflation discussion in February 2025, to a detailed but uncertain qualitative assessment in June 2025, to a retrospective confirmation that tariffs contributed to the 2025 goods inflation upturn in July 2026. None of the three reports provides a single quantitative estimate (e.g., basis points or percentage points) of tariffs' contribution to the overall price level.

**February 7, 2025 MPR: No explicit tariff-inflation link**
The February 2025 report contains no dedicated section or quantitative estimate of tariffs' effect on inflation, and its inflation outlook (core goods, housing services, core nonhousing services) does not cite tariffs as a risk [D24][D32]. Tariffs appear only in financial-market contexts: emerging market fund outflows in Q4 2024 partly reflected "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." [D2], and some market participants pointed to "potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar" higher [D17]. The only import-price-related quantitative statement is that core goods inflation "received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year," but the report does not attribute that increase to tariffs [D24].

**June 20, 2025 MPR: Tariffs as an uncertain but emerging driver of goods inflation**
The June 2025 report's central qualitative assessment is that the effects of the 2025 import tariff increases on U.S. consumer prices are "highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond" [D13]. Key points:
- Tariff effects "cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics," but the pattern of net price changes among goods categories "suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with average monthly price changes for durable goods with tariff exposure (household appliances, consumer electronics) "somewhat strong" since early 2025, while new motor vehicle prices had not risen particularly strongly [D13].
- Domestic steel and aluminum producer prices rose substantially relative to global benchmark prices, "likely reflecting the effects of tariffs" [D13].
- Nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) rose only modestly, suggesting foreign producers had not offset tariffs by cutting prices to U.S. importers [D13].
- Firms widely reported on ISM and regional Fed surveys that input prices had "moved sharply higher this year," many linking this to tariffs [D49].
- Shorter-term inflation expectations "risen considerably this year," with the University of Michigan 12-month median rising from 2.8% (December) to 5.1% (June), "with almost two-thirds of respondents citing tariff-related concerns"; the Michigan 5–10 year median rose from 3% to 4.1%, while longer-term expectations (SPF, Blue Chip, TIPS) remained well anchored [D15][D47].
- The Summary noted household and business sentiment declined "amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" [D33].
- Real imports surged at a historically high 43% annual rate in Q1 2025, "arguably reflects that U.S. businesses pulled forward their imports in anticipation of higher tariffs," with goods imports falling sharply in April after many tariffs were raised [D38].
- The report cites two recent studies (Minton & Somale 2025, FEDS Notes; Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez 2025, working paper) as "recent economic analysis" of tariff effects on consumer prices, but provides no single quantitative pass-through estimate itself [D13].

**July 10, 2026 MPR: Retrospective confirmation of a tariff contribution to 2025 goods inflation**
The July 2026 report looks back on 2025 and confirms a tariff contribution, while noting the 2026 outlook is different:
- The Summary lists "earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" as one of three factors behind higher measured prices (alongside the energy shock and AI-related demand) [D28].
- Inflation "moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods"; total PCE rose 4.1% and core PCE 3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026 [D7][D10].
- "The pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with higher average monthly price increases in high-import-content categories (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends; PCE core goods inflation was 2.4% in May 2026 vs. 0.6% a year earlier [D3][D12].
- The 2026 rise in electronics prices was explicitly NOT tariff-driven, because "most of these products are exempt from tariffs" and the gains reflected AI/semiconductor demand [D12].
- Tariffs also contributed to the step-up in food price inflation (food prices rose 2.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026, up from 1.8% a year earlier) [D11].
- On the 2026 outlook, prices paid by domestic importers (which include tariffs) are estimated to have decreased, "primarily reflect[ing] a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate following February's Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many prevailing tariff measures and whose repeal was only partially offset by new, alternative tariff measures" [D18][D36].
- Short-term inflation expectations (Michigan 12-month) rose from 3.4% (February) to 4.6% (June 2026), "an elevated rate that was nevertheless still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" [D20][D39].
- Internationally, U.S. tariffs were a headwind to foreign growth, with "U.S. sectoral tariffs continuing to weigh on manufacturing" in Mexico and Canada, though foreign inflation rises were attributed mainly to energy [D40][D41][D44].

**Summary table**

| Report | Tariff-inflation characterization | Quantitative estimate? | Key data points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feb 7, 2025 | No explicit tariff-inflation link; tariffs mentioned only in financial-market contexts (dollar, EME flows) | No | Nonfuel import prices +2.4% over the year (not attributed to tariffs) [D24][D2][D17] |
| Jun 20, 2025 | "Highly uncertain"; tariffs "may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation"; input costs "sharply higher" | No (defers to Minton & Somale 2025; Cavallo et al. 2025) | Michigan 12-mo median 2.8%→5.1%; 5–10 yr 3%→4.1%; Q1 2025 real imports +43% annual rate [D13][D49][D15][D47][D38] |
| Jul 10, 2026 | Tariffs "contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases" in 2025; 2026 electronics gains not tariff-driven; 2026 importer prices down after Supreme Court ruling | No | Core goods PCE 2.4% (May 2026) vs 0.6% a year earlier; food +2.4% vs 1.8%; Michigan 12-mo 3.4%→4.6% (below 2025 tariff peak) [D3][D12][D11][D20][D39][D18][D36] |

data.answer: The February 7, 2025 Monetary Policy Report (MPR) contains only limited, indirect discussion of tariffs and their inflation impact — no dedicated section or quantitative tariff-inflation estimate appears in the report. The report notes that core goods inflation "received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year" [D24], a channel through which tariffs could operate, but it does not attribute that increase to tariffs. In the International Developments section, the report mentions tariffs twice in financial-market contexts: (1) EME fund outflows in Q4 2024 partly reflected "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." [D2], and (2) some market participants pointed to "potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar" higher [D17]. The report's inflation outlook discussion (core goods, housing services, core nonhousing services) makes no explicit reference to tariffs as an inflation risk, and the Summary of Economic Projections section does not tie its risk-weighting diffusion indexes to tariffs.
key_facts: Core goods inflation received a small boost last year from price gains in nonfuel import prices, which rose 2.4 percent over the year (figure 6) — the only import-price-related quantitative statement, not explicitly attributed to tariffs [D24].
EME fund outflows in Q4 2024 reflected, among other factors, 'the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S.' [D2].
Some market participants pointed to 'potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports as a factor pushing the dollar' higher [D17].
The report's inflation outlook (core goods, housing services, core nonhousing services) and SEP risk-weighting discussion do not explicitly cite tariffs as an inflation risk [D24][D32][D25].
data.gaps: The report appears to contain no quantitative estimate of tariffs' effect on inflation and no explicit qualitative assessment of tariffs as an inflation driver; the only tariff mentions found are in financial-market contexts (dollar strength, EME fund flows). I could not exhaustively verify every page of the 83-page PDF (e.g., the Monetary Policy section pp. 49-58 and Box 7 on forecast uncertainty), so a brief tariff reference in those sections cannot be fully ruled out.

data.answer: The July 10, 2026 Monetary Policy Report discusses tariffs' impact on inflation in several places, but it offers no explicit quantitative estimate (e.g., percentage-point contribution) of tariffs to inflation. Qualitatively, the report says tariff increases "contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases" in 2025, with price gains concentrated in high-import-content goods categories (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends [D3][D12]. The Summary lists "earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" as one of three factors behind higher measured prices (alongside the energy shock and AI-related demand) [D28]. Tariffs also contributed to the step-up in food price inflation (food prices rose 2.4% over the 12 months ending May, up from 1.8% a year earlier) [D11]. The report notes that the 2026 rise in electronics prices was NOT tariff-driven because most high-tech goods are exempt from tariffs [D12]. On the outlook side, prices paid by domestic importers (which include tariffs) are estimated to have decreased in 2026, reflecting a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate after February's Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, only partially offset by new alternative tariffs [D18][D36]. Short-term inflation expectations peaked following last year's tariff announcements (Michigan 12-month expectations rose from 3.4% in February to 4.6% in June 2026, still well below that tariff-driven peak) [D20][D39]. Internationally, U.S. tariffs weighed on foreign growth (Mexico, Canada) and were a headwind to foreign activity, though foreign inflation rises were attributed mainly to energy [D40][D41][D44].
key_facts: Summary: 'Among the factors contributing to higher measured prices are earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods, a surge in energy prices... and increased demand for some high-tech products' [D28]

p.13: 'measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods'; total PCE rose 4.1% and core PCE 3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026 [D7][D10]

p.15: 'the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases'; average monthly price increases were higher in goods categories more exposed to tariffs due to high import content (household appliances, consumer electronics) relative to pre-tariff trends; PCE core goods inflation was 2.4% in May vs 0.6% a year earlier [D3][D12]
p.15: early-2026 gains in software/computers/electronics prices reflect AI/semiconductor demand, not tariffs, since 'most of these products are exempt from tariffs' [D12]
p.14: step-up in food price inflation (2.4% over 12 months ending May, up from 1.8%) includes 'the effects of higher tariffs and increases in agricultural and livestock commodity prices' [D11]

p.16: prices paid by domestic producers to import products (which include tariffs) are estimated to have decreased in 2026, 'primarily reflect[ing] a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate following February's Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many prevailing tariff measures and whose repeal was only partially offset by new, alternative tariff measures' [D18][D36]

p.18: Michigan 12-month inflation expectations rose from 3.4% (Feb) to 4.6% (June 2026), 'an elevated rate that was nevertheless still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases' [D20][D39]
pp.11, 41: U.S. tariffs were a headwind to foreign economic activity in H1 2026; 'U.S. sectoral tariffs continuing to weigh on manufacturing' in Mexico and Canada [D40][D41][D44]
data.gaps: The report contains no explicit quantitative estimate (e.g., percentage-point contribution) of tariffs to inflation; all tariff-inflation statements are qualitative. I did not exhaustively scan the Monetary Policy section (pp. 45-52), the SEP narrative (pp. 53-68), or the special topics boxes for additional tariff-inflation passages, so minor mentions there may be missed.

data.answer: The June 20, 2025 Monetary Policy Report discusses tariffs' impact on inflation primarily in its "Domestic Developments" inflation section (pp. 17–20) and in the Summary (p. 11). The report's central qualitative assessment is that the effects of the 2025 import tariff increases on U.S. consumer prices are "highly uncertain" because trade policy continues to evolve and it is "still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond." It notes that tariff effects "cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics," but the pattern of net price changes among goods categories "suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation" — specifically, average monthly price changes for durable goods with tariff exposure (household appliances, consumer electronics) have been "somewhat strong" since early 2025, while new motor vehicle prices have not risen particularly strongly despite tariff exposure. The report also finds that domestic steel and aluminum producer prices have risen substantially relative to global benchmark prices, "likely reflecting the effects of tariffs," and that nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) have risen only modestly, suggesting foreign producers have not offset tariffs by cutting prices to U.S. importers. Firms widely report on business surveys (ISM, regional Fed surveys) that input prices have moved "sharply higher" this year, many linking this to tariffs. On inflation expectations, the report states that shorter-term expectations have "risen considerably this year," with the University of Michigan 12-month median rising from 2.8% (December) to 5.1% (June), with "almost two-thirds of respondents citing tariff-related concerns"; the Michigan 5–10 year median rose from 3% to 4.1%. Longer-term expectations (SPF, Blue Chip, TIPS) remain well anchored. The Summary notes household and business sentiment declined "amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment." The report provides no single quantitative estimate of the tariff pass-through to the overall price level; it cites two recent studies (Minton & Somale 2025, FEDS Notes; Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez 2025, working paper) as "recent economic analysis" of tariff effects on consumer prices.

That said, price changes so far this year have not been particularly strong for new motor vehicles\" (p. 17) [D13]", "\"prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum have risen substantially relative to the global prices, on net, over this period, likely reflecting the effects of tariffs\" (p. 17) [D13]", "\"nonfuel import prices—which measure the prices paid to foreign producers and exclude tariffs—have increased modestly so far this year, suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers\" (p. 17) [D13]", "\"domestic firms widely report on business surveys that they have faced increases in input cost pressures this year, which many firms have linked to higher tariffs\" — ISM and regional Fed surveys show input prices \"moved sharply higher this year\" (pp. 17–18) [D13][D49]", "\"measures of household and business sentiment have declined this year amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment as well as heightened uncertainty about the economic outlook\" (Summary, p. 11) [D33]", "\"Although measures of shorter-term inflation expectations have moved sharply higher this year, reflecting concerns around tariffs, most measures of longer-term inflation expectations have remained within the range of values seen in the decade before the pandemic\" (Summary, p. 11) [D33]", "Michigan survey: median 12-month inflation expectation rose from 2.8% (Dec) to 5.1% (June), \"with almost two-thirds of respondents citing tariff-related concerns\"; data.answer:
Taking "Monetary Policy Reports from February 2025 to July 2026" to mean the three MPRs available in that window—February 7, 2025; June 20, 2025; and July 10, 2026—the reports show a clear evolution: from no explicit tariff-inflation discussion in February 2025, to a detailed but uncertain qualitative assessment in June 2025, to a retrospective confirmation that tariffs contributed to the 2025 goods inflation upturn in July 2026. question: What changes to the Federal Reserve Board's membership and leadership happened between January 2025 and September 2026?
answer:
Between January 2025 and September 2026, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors saw a change in its Vice Chair for Supervision (Michael S. Barr stepped down, replaced by Michelle W. Bowman), the departure of one governor (Adriana D. Kugler), the appointment and subsequent resignation of a short-term member (Stephen I. Miran), and a change in the Chair (Jerome H. Powell's term ended and Kevin Warsh was sworn in as the new Chairman) [D1][D2][D3][D5][D7][D9][D15][D17].

The specific personnel changes, in chronological order, are:

*   **January 6, 2025:** Michael S. Barr announced he would step down as Vice Chair for Supervision, effective February 28, 2025, or earlier upon a successor's confirmation; he continued to serve as a governor [D15].
*   **March 17, 2025:** Governor Michelle W. Bowman issued a statement thanking President Trump for nominating her as Vice Chair for Supervision [D7].
*   **June 9, 2025:** Michelle W. Bowman was sworn in as Vice Chair for Supervision by Chair Jerome H. Powell; she had been nominated on March 24, 2025, and confirmed by the Senate on June 4, 2025 [D2].
*   **August 1, 2025:** Adriana D. Kugler submitted her resignation as governor, effective August 8, 2025 [D17].
*   **September 16, 2025:** Stephen I. Miran was sworn in as a Board member by Judge Elizabeth L. Branch; he had been nominated on September 2, 2025, and confirmed by the Senate on September 15, 2025 [D1].
*   **May 14, 2026:** Stephen I. Miran submitted his resignation as a Board member, effective when or shortly before his successor was sworn in [D9].
*   **May 15, 2026:** The Board named Jerome H. Powell as chair pro tempore to serve until Kevin M. Warsh was sworn in as the new chair [D5].
*   **May 22, 2026:** Kevin Warsh took the oath of office as chairman and a member of the Board of Governors; he had been nominated on March 4, 2026, and confirmed by the Senate as a member on May 12, 2026, and as chairman on May 13, 2026; the FOMC unanimously selected him as its chairman [D3].

question: What did the Fed decide at its last meeting?
answer:
Taking "last meeting" to mean the most recent FOMC meeting, September 15–16, 2026: the Federal Reserve decided to **raise** the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to **3-3/4 to 4 percent** (from 3.50%–3.75%), in a **unanimous 12–0 vote** [D1][W2][W12][W13]. This was the Fed's first rate hike since July 2023 and the first tightening move since the easing cycle began in September 2024 [W6][W22]. The Committee also **continued its policy of maintaining ample reserves** in the banking system, i.e., no change to balance sheet policy [D1][D5].

**Rationale (statement and press conference)**
- The statement cited economic activity expanding at a solid pace, resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth, robust capital investment, and job gains keeping pace with the workforce, with the unemployment rate changing little; it noted elevated uncertainty owing in part to geopolitical developments [D1].
- The core reason for the hike was that "inflation remains elevated," and the action was taken to support "a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal," with the statement adding, "The Committee will deliver price stability" [D1].
- In his press conference, Chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation has run above target for more than five years, that summer readings did not show underlying trends meaningfully improved (12-month total PCE likely ~3.6% in August, core PCE ~3.2%, CPI ~2.4%), and that the Committee's standard for action—confidence that underlying inflation is moving to the 2% objective clearly and at sufficient speed—"has not been satisfied" [D6]. He framed the move as "removing a dose of accommodation" rather than the start of an aggressive tightening cycle, and said the unanimous vote showed "resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis" [D5][D8][W14].

**Forward path and market reaction**
- The SEP dot plot signaled further tightening: the median projected federal funds rate for end-2026 rose from 3.8% (June) to 4.1%, implying at least one more 25bp hike by year-end; 16 of 18 policymakers expected at least one additional hike in 2026 [W9][W11][D3].
- Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5% (to ~5.016%) and the 2-year yield rose to ~4.74%, with stocks pulling back and the dollar strengthening [W23][W24]. Analysts noted the 25bp move was largely priced in, with the bigger driver being Warsh's hawkish tone and the dot plot; Goldman Sachs' Kay Haigh expected the Fed to skip October and hike again in December, and MUFG similarly forecast a December hike while doubting the full FOMC shared Warsh's hawkish bias [W23][W14]. question: What did the Beige Book say about Chicago?
answer:
Taking "the Beige Book" to mean the most recent edition, the September 2026 report (released September 2, 2026), the Chicago (Seventh) District section describes a modest, broad-based improvement: economic activity increased slightly in July and early August, with contacts expecting a similar pace over the next 12 months [D1].

**Overall characterization**
- Economic activity up slightly; manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment up slightly; consumer spending and construction/real estate flat on balance; business spending declined slightly; nonbusiness contacts saw no change [D1].
- Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened slightly [D1].

**Labor markets and wages**
- Employment rose slightly, with hiring expected to continue at a similar pace; layoff rates remained low and turnover in leisure/hospitality was little [D1].
- Some tightening: trucking driver supply pulled back after recent federal regulation changes, and wage increases were large in certain skilled trades such as electricians [D1].
- Outside the trades, wages and benefits costs were up modestly [D1].

**Prices and inflation**
- Prices rose moderately overall, with a similar pace expected over the next 12 months; producer prices rose modestly [D1].
- Nonlabor input costs were up modestly, slower than the moderate pace in the prior report; price increases were reported in raw materials, energy, and shipping, with shippers continuing to add fuel surcharges [D1].
- Consumer prices rose moderately; one retail analyst expected some retailers to use tariff refunds to offset freight surcharges or fund promotions [D1].

**Consumer spending**
- Flat on balance; more consumers were trading down to discount stores and warehouse clubs, including higher-income customers shopping at discount furniture stores [D2].
- Leisure/hospitality spending decreased on net: hotel room demand was up, but restaurant traffic slowed due to higher food and gas prices [D2].
- New light vehicle sales held steady, though some dealers noted decreased sales to small businesses [D2].

**Business spending**
- Decreased slightly, with a small decline in capital expenditures but expectations for a small increase next year [D2].
- Holiday-season orders were lower than last year; manufacturing inventories were a little high; a few contacts reported shortages or long lead times for aluminum, copper, and steel [D2].

**Manufacturing**
- Demand increased modestly: primary metals sales rose slightly from an already high level; fabricated metals production grew modestly including in defense; machinery sales rose modestly on stronger defense orders; auto production ticked up and heavy-truck production increased slightly [D3].

**Construction and real estate**
- Flat on balance; residential construction was unchanged, with higher land costs dampening single-family homebuilding, and multifamily starts postponed due to higher costs and tighter credit [D2].
- Data center and other mega-site projects remained the main centers of activity—one contact said "without data centers, construction would be in a recession"—while commercial real estate activity rose slightly on strong industrial and big-box warehouse demand [D2].

**Banking and finance**
- Financial conditions tightened slightly: bond values edged down, equity values rose moderately, and volatility was flat and low [D3].
- Business loan volumes increased slightly (with greater M&A activity), loan quality edged down, and rates rose modestly; consumer loan volumes decreased modestly, partly due to high interest rates, and residential mortgage demand was soft [D3].
- Several lenders reported elevated consumer uncertainty due to the conflict in the Middle East [D3].

**Agriculture**
- Farm income expectations for 2026 improved some from a low level; crops were mostly in good shape despite some stress from heavy rains and flooding, with corn and soybean yields expected close to record levels [D3].
- Corn, soybean, and wheat prices increased on stronger demand; biofuel demand boosted ethanol and biodiesel production; egg and hog prices rose, dairy prices fell, and cattle prices decreased further, with a key meat packing plant's abrupt closure adding challenges for cattle producers [D3].
- Diesel prices rose, but many fertilizer prices fell [D3].

**Community conditions**
- No change overall; contacts highlighted continued price pressures from the Middle East conflict and a mixed labor market (some hiring difficulty, others cutting hours) [D3][D4].
- State government contacts reported strong sales and income tax revenues; service-oriented small businesses struggled to pass on cost increases, while manufacturing clients were resilient and nonprofit donations held steady [D3][D4].

question: Summarize the latest FOMC minutes.
answer:
Taking "the latest FOMC minutes" to mean the minutes of the July 28–29, 2026 FOMC meeting (the most recent minutes in the collection): the Committee voted 9–3 to hold the federal funds target range at 3½–3¾ percent, with three members dissenting in favor of a 25 basis point hike [D11][D12].

## Policy decision and vote
- Nine members agreed to maintain the target range at 3½–3¾ percent and reaffirmed the policy of maintaining ample reserves; three members—Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan—voted against, preferring a 25 basis point increase [D11][D12].
- The postmeeting statement was approved by a 9–3 vote and retained the June language that the Committee "will deliver price stability," which almost all members supported [D11][D12].
- The statement noted economic activity expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty tied in part to the Middle East conflict, strong productivity and capital investment, job gains keeping pace with the workforce, and inflation remaining elevated relative to the 2 percent goal, partly reflecting supply shocks including energy [D12].
- Consistent with the hold, the Board of Governors unanimously kept the interest rate paid on reserve balances at 3.65 percent and the primary credit rate at 3.75 percent, effective July 30, 2026 [D12][D13].

## Assessment of the economy
- Inflation: total PCE inflation was 4.1 percent in May and core PCE 3.4 percent, both higher than a year earlier, attributed to past tariff increases, higher energy/input costs from the Middle East conflict, and AI-buildout demand; the staff estimated total PCE stepped down to 3.7 percent in June (led by lower consumer energy prices) and core edged down [D3][D4].
- Labor market: the unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in June, little changed over the prior two years; payroll gains strengthened in the first half of 2026, and average hourly earnings rose 3.5 percent year over year, down 0.4 percentage point from a year earlier; participants saw labor demand and supply in balance [D4][D8].
- Growth: real GDP slowed in the second quarter, but real private domestic final purchases picked up and rose faster than GDP; consumer spending firmed and the AI buildout supported business investment; the staff projected real GDP to slightly outpace potential next year, with risks to growth skewed to the downside and risks to inflation skewed to the upside [D4][D7].

## Key debate on the path of policy
- Most participants supported holding the target range, reasoning that information accumulating over the intermeeting period would reduce uncertainty about the inflation outlook [D10].
- Several participants favored a 25 basis point hike, judging price pressures broad-based and arguing that acting now would help forestall a steeper, potentially more costly sequence of tightening later [D10][D11].
- Many assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and some noted financial conditions might not yet be sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to 2 percent [D10].

## Dissents and differing views
- The three dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) preferred a 25 basis point increase at this meeting [D11][D12].
- Views differed on AI's price effects: some saw limited effects so far, others saw broader demand-driven price effects already or soon, and a few noted it was too early to tell whether AI would mainly shift relative prices or raise inflation more broadly; some also expected eventual productivity gains to put downward pressure on inflation [D8].
- A few participants noted lingering labor-market softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment) and upside risks to wage growth [D8][D9].

## Other significant topics
- Financial stability: the staff characterized vulnerabilities as "notable," with the equity premium at levels only lower during the dot-com bubble, hedge-fund leverage near all-time highs, and rising private credit redemption requests; participants focused on AI-infrastructure financing, high equity valuations, private credit, and Treasury-market volatility [D5][D6][D9][D10].
- Balance sheet: most participants commented, noting the task-force findings would be a useful input for a future comprehensive discussion; issues included market functioning, financial stability, and Treasury maturity composition, and many reaffirmed the target range as the primary policy tool [D11].
- Meeting schedule: the Chairman (Kevin Warsh) suggested six meetings per year would allow more information to accumulate; no decision was made and the 2026 schedule was unchanged [D11].
- Market context: investors priced about a one-in-three chance of a July hike and a full 25 basis point hike by September, while the Desk survey median expected no change this year or next and a cut in early 2028 [D2].
- Next meeting: September 15–16, 2026 [D13].

Note: the evidence covers the full minutes of the July 28–29, 2026 meeting; no other meeting's minutes are included here.

Participants judged inflation remained elevated (total PCE at 4.1% in May, core 3.4%; both estimated to have eased in June), the labor market stable (unemployment 4.2%), and activity expanding at a solid pace supported by AI investment and resilient consumer spending [D3][D4][D7][D8][D9]. The key debate was whether to hike now: several participants favored a 25 bp increase, arguing price pressures were broad-based and that acting now would forestall a steeper, costlier tightening later, while most preferred to wait for more information given the short interval since June [D10][D11]. The statement retained the June "will deliver price stability" language, which almost all members supported [D11]. Other topics included balance sheet policy (task-force findings to inform a future comprehensive discussion), the Chairman's suggestion of six meetings per year, and financial stability concerns centered on AI-infrastructure financing, high equity valuations, private credit, and hedge-fund leverage [D6][D9][D10][D11].
key_facts: Policy decision: 9 members agreed to maintain the target range at 3½–3¾ percent and reaffirm ample reserves; 3 members (Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, Lorie K. Logan) voted against, preferring a 25 bp increase [D11][D12].

Statement released by 9–3 vote: 'Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East... Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal... The Committee will deliver price stability.' [D12].

Inflation: total PCE 4.1% (May), core PCE 3.4%; staff estimated total PCE stepped down to 3.7% in June and core edged down; drivers included tariffs, Middle East energy costs, and AI buildout demand [D3][D4][D7].

Labor market: unemployment 4.2% in June, little changed over two years; payroll gains strengthened in H1 2026; average hourly earnings +3.5% y/y, down 0.4 pp from a year earlier; participants saw demand and supply in balance [D4][D8].

Growth: real GDP slowed in Q2 but private domestic final purchases picked up; consumer spending firmed; AI buildout supported business investment; staff projected GDP to slightly outpace potential next year [D4][D6][D7][D9].

Debate: several participants favored a 25 bp hike, judging price pressures broad-based and that a hike would help forestall a steeper, more costly tightening later; most supported holding, citing the short interval since June and the value of more information [D10][D11].

Financial stability: staff characterized vulnerabilities as 'notable'; equity premium at levels only lower during the dot-com bubble; hedge-fund leverage near all-time highs; private credit redemption requests rising; SLOOS showed standards easing for a fourth straight quarter [D5][D6][D9][D10].

Market context: investors priced ~1-in-3 chance of a July hike and a full 25 bp hike by September; Desk survey median expected no change this year or next, a cut in early 2028 [D2].
Next meeting: September 15–16, 2026; IORB set at 3.65%, primary credit rate 3.75% [D12][D13].

data.answer:
Taking "the latest FOMC minutes" to mean the minutes of the July 28–29, 2026 FOMC meeting (the most recent minutes in the collection): the Committee voted 9–3 to hold the federal funds target range at 3½–3¾ percent, with three members dissenting in favor of a 25 basis point hike [D11][D12].

## Policy decision and vote
- Nine members agreed to maintain the target range at 3½–3¾ percent and reaffirmed the policy of maintaining ample reserves; three members—Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan—voted against, preferring a 25 basis point increase [D11][D12].
- The postmeeting statement was approved by a 9–3 vote and retained the June language that the Committee "will deliver price stability," which almost all members supported [D11][D12].
- The statement noted economic activity expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty tied in part to the Middle East conflict, strong productivity and capital investment, job gains keeping pace with the workforce, and inflation remaining elevated relative to the 2 percent goal, partly reflecting supply shocks including energy [D12].
- Consistent with the hold, the Board of Governors unanimously kept the interest rate paid on reserve balances at 3.65 percent and the primary credit rate at 3.75 percent, effective July 30, 2026 [D12][D13].

## Assessment of the economy
- Inflation: total PCE inflation was 4.1 percent in May and core PCE 3.4 percent, both higher than a year earlier, attributed to past tariff increases, higher energy/input costs from the Middle East conflict, and AI-buildout demand; the staff estimated total PCE stepped down to 3.7 percent in June (led by lower consumer energy prices) and core edged down [D3][D4].
- Labor market: the unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in June, little changed over the prior two years; payroll gains strengthened in the first half of 2026, and average hourly earnings rose 3.5 percent year over year, down 0.4 percentage point from a year earlier; participants saw labor demand and supply in balance [D4][D8].
- Growth: real GDP slowed in the second quarter, but real private domestic final purchases picked up and rose faster than GDP; consumer spending firmed and the AI buildout supported business investment; the staff projected real GDP to slightly outpace potential next year, with risks to growth skewed to the downside and risks to inflation skewed to the upside [D4][D7].

## Key debate on the path of policy
- Most participants supported holding the target range, reasoning that information accumulating over the intermeeting period would reduce uncertainty about the inflation outlook [D10].
- Several participants favored a 25 basis point hike, judging price pressures broad-based and arguing that acting now would help forestall a steeper, potentially more costly sequence of tightening later [D10][D11].
- Many assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and some noted financial conditions might not yet be sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to 2 percent [D10].

## Dissents and differing views
- The three dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) preferred a 25 basis point increase at this meeting [D11][D12].
- Views differed on AI's price effects: some saw limited effects so far, others saw broader demand-driven price effects already or soon, and a few noted it was too early to tell whether AI would mainly shift relative prices or raise inflation more broadly; some also expected eventual productivity gains to put downward pressure on inflation [D8].
- A few participants noted lingering labor-market softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment) and upside risks to wage growth [D8][D9].

## Other significant topics
- Financial stability: the staff characterized vulnerabilities as "notable," with the equity premium at levels only lower during the dot-com bubble, hedge-fund leverage near all-time highs, and rising private credit redemption requests; participants focused on AI-infrastructure financing, high equity valuations, private credit, and Treasury-market volatility [D5][D6][D9][D10].
- Balance sheet: most participants commented, noting the task-force findings would be a useful input for a future comprehensive discussion; issues included market functioning, financial stability, and Treasury maturity composition, and many reaffirmed the target range as the primary policy tool [D11].
- Meeting schedule: the Chairman (Kevin Warsh) suggested six meetings per year would allow more information to accumulate; no decision was made and the 2026 schedule was unchanged [D11].
- Market context: investors priced about a one-in-three chance of a July hike and a full 25 basis point hike by September, while the Desk survey median expected no change this year or next and a cut in early 2028 [D2].
- Next meeting: September 15–16, 2026 [D13].

Note: the evidence covers the full minutes of the July 28–29, 2026 meeting; no other meeting's minutes are included here.
