Taking "over 2026" to mean the 2026 FOMC meetings, minutes, projections, and 2026 speeches/testimony available in the collection: the Federal Reserve's view of the labor market improved steadily over the year, moving from a "weak/fragile, possibly still softening" assessment in early 2026, to "stabilizing" in spring, to "stable and consistent with full employment" by summer and fall. The dominant policy concern shifted from downside employment risk to inflation, culminating in a 25-basis-point rate hike on September 16, 2026. (Note: the January 28, March 18, and April 29, 2026 press conferences were delivered by Chair Jerome Powell; Kevin Warsh became Chair and first held a press conference on June 17, 2026.)

## FOMC statements: from "low job gains" to "kept pace with the workforce"

The Committee's official characterization of the labor market improved over the year, while the unemployment rate was consistently described as stable and never flagged as elevated. Wage growth was not mentioned in any 2026 statement.

| Meeting | Labor-market language in statement | Policy decision |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 28, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has shown some signs of stabilization." [D80] | Hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (Miran and Waller dissented, preferring a cut) [D80] |
| Mar 18, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months." [D81] | Hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (Miran dissented, preferring a cut) [D81] |
| Apr 29, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, on average, and the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months." [D82] | Hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (Miran dissented for a cut; Hammack, Kashkari, Logan dissented over easing-bias language) [D82] |
| Jun 17, 2026 | "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little." [D77] | Hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (12–0) [D77] |
| Jul 29, 2026 | "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little." [D78] | Hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (9–3; Hammack, Kashkari, Logan preferred a hike) [D78] |
| Sep 16, 2026 | "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little." [D79] | RAISE by 1/4 point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent (12–0) [D79] |

The "balance of risks"/"attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate" language appeared in the January–April statements but was dropped from the June–September statements, which instead emphasized that "the Committee will deliver price stability" [D80][D81][D82][D77][D78][D79].

## Minutes: from peak downside concern (Mar–Apr) to confidence in stability (Jun–Jul)

Participants' assessment evolved from cautious stabilization (January), through peak concern about downside employment risk (March–April), to a clear recovery in confidence (June–July):

- **Jan 28, 2026:** Unemployment held steady with low job gains; conditions "may be stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling"; both layoffs and hiring low; business contacts cautious on hiring due to AI/uncertainty; the vast majority judged downside risks had "diminished" though most noted they "remained" [D24]. Staff: unemployment 4.4% in December, average hourly earnings (AHE) +3.8% y/y [D62].
- **Mar 18, 2026:** Unemployment little changed, job gains low; several highlighted softening (slight rise in prime-age unemployment, job growth concentrated in health care, declining job-availability surveys); the vast majority judged employment risks "skewed to the downside," with "upside risks to inflation and downside risks to employment both elevated" [D12][D38][D14]. Staff: unemployment 4.4% in February, AHE +3.8% [D65].
- **Apr 29, 2026:** Unemployment little changed, job gains low on average; most judged stabilization, with low job growth "not necessarily indicative of fragility" (a few saw it as fragility); signs of softness included sector concentration, declining job availability, and "modest rate of wage growth"; most judged employment risks "tilted to the downside," while the vast majority saw increased risk inflation takes longer to reach 2% [D16][D86].
- **Jun 17, 2026:** Unemployment "relatively stable over the past year" near longer-run level; payroll gains "strengthened this year"; job openings, claims, layoffs stable—a "balanced labor market"; "concerns earlier this year about labor market deterioration had eased," with downside employment risks having "moderated a bit" even as upside inflation risks "remained elevated" [D30][D31][D20]. Staff: AHE +3.4% in May [D61].
- **Jul 29, 2026:** Labor market "stable, with labor demand and supply in balance"; payroll gains strengthened and broadened beyond health care; the market had "strengthened modestly"; a few noted lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment); nominal wage growth "moderate and consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent"; AI-related layoff fears "had not materialized" [D22][D23][D35]. Staff: unemployment 4.2% in June, AHE +3.5% [D32].

## Projections: end-2026 unemployment forecast fell steadily

The Committee's median projection for the end-2026 unemployment rate declined at each of the three 2026 meetings that released Summary of Economic Projections (the FOMC publishes projections only at March, June, September, and December meetings, so no projections exist for the January 28, April 29, or July 29, 2026 meetings):

| SEP release | Median end-2026 unemployment |
|---|---|
| Mar 18, 2026 | 4.4% [D33][D34][D67] |
| Jun 17, 2026 | 4.3% [D33][D34][D68] |
| Sep 16, 2026 | 4.1% [D33][D34][D72] |

This 0.3 percentage-point cumulative decline (4.4% → 4.3% → 4.1%) quantifies a progressively more optimistic labor-market outlook. For context, the December 10, 2025 release had projected 4.4% for end-2026, and 2025 actual unemployment was 4.5% [D34]. By the September 16, 2026 SEP, the median end-2026, 2027, 2028, and 2029 unemployment projections were all 4.1%, with the longer-run projection at 4.2% [D72].
